news_drafts.headline: Edinburgh forecasts £8.615m council-wide overspend at month three; levy-funded culture projects face December review
news_drafts.lead:
The City of Edinburgh Council is projecting an overspend of £8.615m across all its services for 2026/27, according to the month-three budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) before the Culture and Communities Committee on 8 October. The figure was first reported to the Finance and Resources Committee on 24 September, and the paper says "an overall overspend of £8.615m is projected".

Within the committee's own area, Parks and Greenspaces is forecasting spending of £0.203m more than its £7.706m budget. The paper attributes this to "additional transport charges and the cost of temporary toilet facilities". Both are running costs rather than a rise in demand or a fall in income.

A separate paper on the Edinburgh Visitor Levy Cultural Programming Fund sets out how that money will be managed. The council will carry out an income review in December 2026, comparing the levy revenue actually collected with projections. If income is lower, the paper says, "a review will be undertaken of the remaining planned expenditure of the financial year to determine whether there is the requirement to pause projects or reduce the financial allocation". In the meantime, projects in the first year are being programmed quarterly ahead of that review.
news_drafts.paper_title: 8.2 - Culture and Communities Committee Revenue Budget Monitoring 202627 – Month Three position

news_drafts.headline: Edinburgh repaid £32m of market debt in 2025-26, including two LOBO loans, at par with no penalty
news_drafts.lead:
City of Edinburgh Council repaid £32m of loans from commercial lenders during 2025-26, including two LOBO loans, according to its treasury management annual report for the year, which went to the Finance and Resources Committee on 24 September. A LOBO loan is a bank loan where, on set dates, the lender may propose a higher interest rate and the council may then repay the loan in full instead of accepting it.

On the two loans, the lenders exercised their option to ask for a higher rate. The council used its own option to repay. The report says the council repaid "at par with no penalty", meaning it paid back the amount it had borrowed and no more. Treasury management is how a council borrows, invests its spare cash and manages the risks of both.

The council still has £122.4m of LOBO borrowing outstanding. The loans fall due between 2028 and 2066, and carry interest rates from 4.375% to 5.25%. The same lender options apply to them on their set dates. The papers give no figure for what the council plans to do about them.

news_drafts.headline: Edinburgh Council's debt service bill rises £8.6m to £86.2m on capital borrowing
news_drafts.lead: Edinburgh Council's external interest costs jumped from £67.2m to £77.5m in 2025-26 as it borrowed £350m to fund capital investment at an average rate of 4.60 per cent. The council's total debt servicing bill — the annual cost of paying back loans — rose to £86.2m from £77.6m a year earlier. The pace of borrowing is placing the Housing Revenue Account, the separate account funded by council house rents, under strain: the council's own figures show debt servicing will consume 64.6 per cent of housing rental income by 2030-31, against 39.2 per cent now. The council borrowed at the shorter end of the market — accepting loans that mature sooner — to achieve rates below budget, but this created additional refinancing risk if short-term borrowing rates spike when these loans mature.

findings.paper_title: 7.6 - Application of Second and Long-Term Empty Home Council Tax Premium Income
findings.headline: Evidence from existing pilot indicates repairs identified through sensor monitoring cost an average of £456, compared with £1,533 through other reporting routes.
findings.detail: The Council tested damp sensors in 500 homes as part of a pilot. Early sensor detection identifies problems requiring cheaper repairs on average. The report cautions that these figures are not directly comparable, but they form part of the evidence base for expanding the sensor program to approximately 27,000 sensors.
findings.matters: The investment case for the sensor program rests on earlier detection reducing repair costs; a finance director would need to understand the robustness of the cost assumptions and whether earlier intervention actually delivers the claimed savings.
findings.figures: Existing pilot: 500 homes; sensor-detected repairs average £456; other reporting routes average £1,533; proposed expansion: approximately 27,000 sensors across 9,000 homes over two years
findings.quote: Evidence from the existing pilot indicates that the average cost of repairs identified through sensor monitoring is £456, compared with £1,533  identified through other reporting routes. Whilst these figures are not directly comparable, they point to the potential benefits of earlier intervention.

findings.paper_title: 7.6 - Application of Second and Long-Term Empty Home Council Tax Premium Income
findings.headline: Investigation and Commencement of Repair (Scotland) Regulations 2026 came into force on 6 October 2026, requiring investigation of damp and mould reports within set timescales.
findings.detail: The new regulations create statutory duties for social and private landlords to investigate and commence repairs within defined timescales. This regulatory requirement drives the investment decision in damp and mould prevention and monitoring in Council homes.
findings.matters: A finance director needs to know the spending decision is underpinned by statutory compliance requirements, not discretionary choice, which affects the flexibility of budget commitments.
findings.quote: The Investigation and Commencement of Repair (Scotland) Regulations 2026 will come into force on 6 October 2026.  From this date, social and private landlords in Scotland will be required to investigate reports of damp or mould and commence any required repairs within set timescales.

findings.paper_title: 7.6 - Application of Second and Long-Term Empty Home Council Tax Premium Income
findings.headline: The sensor monitoring program would create a £0.5m annual maintenance liability with no identified funding source.
findings.detail: Installation of damp sensors across approximately 9,000 Council homes is projected to cost up to £4m over two years, plus staffing. The report identifies an additional annual maintenance cost of £0.5m and future battery replacement costs in around ten years, but explicitly states no budgetary provision exists for these costs, creating an ongoing commitment without identified funding.
findings.matters: Capital programs should have identified funding for all lifecycle costs before approval; an identified £0.5m annual liability without a funding source represents a future budget pressure.
findings.figures: Up to £4m capital investment over two years; £0.5m annual maintenance liability; battery replacement needed in approximately ten years
findings.quote: installation of sensors would entail an additional annual maintenance liability of £0.5m, as well as a need to provide for battery replacement in around ten years' time.  At present, no budgetary provision exists for these costs.

findings.paper_title: 7.6 - Application of Second and Long-Term Empty Home Council Tax Premium Income
findings.headline: The additional premium income depends on behavioral change to reduce empty homes, which if successful would reduce the projected income below the £4m estimate.
findings.detail: The policy intent is to bring long-term and second empty homes back into use through the tax penalty. If the premium achieves this goal, fewer homes will be liable to the premium, generating less income than projected. The report explicitly warns that sums newly committed risk being higher than the funding source if income falls short.
findings.matters: A finance director must evaluate whether commitments based on projected income are sustainable if that income does not materialize; this creates a risk that capital spending exceeds its funding source.
findings.figures: Estimated additional income of £4m in 2027/28 and 2028/29, but dependent on behavioral change reducing the number of empty homes
findings.quote: A key driver of the higher premium is effecting behavioural change to increase overall housing supply, the result of which would see fewer long-term empty and/or second homes in the city.  This, by extension, would reduce the overall level of additional income generated.

findings.paper_title: 7.6 - Application of Second and Long-Term Empty Home Council Tax Premium Income
findings.headline: Allocating £4m new premium income to housing projects would increase the incremental savings gap from £14.3m to £18.3m in 2027/28.
findings.detail: The Council already assumed the new premium income as part of setting the 2026/27 budget. Dedicating it to new housing spending means the funding is unavailable to close the identified savings gap in 2027/28, widening that gap by the full amount of the new income.
findings.matters: A finance director must understand that new revenue committed to new spending does not reduce budget pressure if it was already factored into existing plans; it adds to the savings challenge.
findings.figures: Current estimated incremental gap £14.3m; with the new commitments £18.3m; additional income estimated at £4m in 2027/28
findings.quote: introducing new commitments in the way suggested in the motion would add up to £4m to the Council's incremental funding gap in 2027/28, increasing it from the current estimate of £14.3m to £18.3m.
